subdivision.heading: Assessment of Costs by Assessment Officer

operative_text.controlling:
10.39(1)  An assessment officer may direct any question arising
about the assessment of costs payable to be referred to the Court
for a decision or direction.
(2)  The assessment officer may do all or any of the following:
(a) require one party to serve another party or other interested
person with notice of the reference;
(b) specify how a reference to the Court is to be prepared and
by whom;
(c) prescribe time limits;
(d) specify any other matter for the effective and efficient
disposition of the reference.
(3)  On considering a question referred to it, the Court may make
any order it considers appropriate in the circumstances, including
an order to enforce a direction given under rule 10.38.

BOOK_A.title: Reference to Court
BOOK_A.operative_text_raw:
10.39(1) An assessment ofﬁcer may direct any question arising about the
assessment of costs payable to be referred to the Court for a decision or
direction.⁷
(2) The assessment ofﬁcer may do all or any of the following:
(a) require one party to serve another party or other interested person
with notice of the reference;
(b) specify how a reference to the Court is to be prepared and by whom;
(c) prescribe time limits;
(d) specify any other matter for the effective and efﬁcient disposition of
the reference.
(3) On considering a question referred to it, the Court may make any order it
considers appropriate in the circumstances, including an order to enforce a
direction given under rule 10.38 [Assessment officer’s authority].
BOOK_A.commentary:
Where an assessment ofﬁcer refers a matter to the court, even if he is then holding a second
assessment after a successful appeal from the ﬁrst assessment, the second hearing in King's
Bench is a trial de novo and not an appeal from the original assessment.¹
A reference to the court of a speciﬁc question about level of costs, by an assessment ofﬁcer,
is no occasion to relitigate whether each party given costs had been entitled to costs.²
Another example of a reference is the Ulrich case.³

BOOK_B.title: Reference to Court

commentary.text: Rule 10.39 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.39. Weighing evidence and interpreting a fee agreement should be referred to a judge under this rule. However, the ground of appeal which presents the principal concern is the clerk's determination that the $5,000.00 paid by the clients was, by agreement between the parties, payment of merely the first sub-account and not, as claimed by the clients, a payment in full of the whole account. To arrive at this finding the clerk must have had to weigh evidence on the nature of the agreement and to interpret it in the light of the evidence. This is clearly a judicial function which by the Rules he, as a purely administrative officer, is not empowered to perform. As an administrative officer he may determine what services were rendered and then proceed to evaluate those services as one who by his daily contact with the profession is qualified to assess their value. It might be thought that this latter function is judicial but in my opinion it is merely an exercise in fact finding. The line of demarcation between the exercise of an administrative function and a judicial function is perhaps lacking in precision or clarity, but to interpret the meaning of an agreement is clearly beyond his power and is just such a matter which the clerk should refer to a judge under Rule 634 (supra). Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd. (1982), 48 A.R. 311 (Q.B.), at 315, per Cormack J. In Linton v. Prusak (1999), 241 A.R. 392 (Q.B.), Wilson J. agreed with Cormack J. in Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd. (1982), 48 A.R. 311 (Q.B.), and said at p. 394: These cases support the proposition taken by Cormack, J., which correctly states the law, in my respectful opinion. In MacKimmie Matthews v. Hector ([1998), 219 A.R. 163 (C.A.)], McFadyen, J.A., had this to say about the powers of the taxation officer (para. 17): The taxation officer is limited to questions relating to a quantum alone and cannot resolve other issues which may arise between the parties. If another issue arises, as it did in this case, the taxation officer refers the question to the court for resolution. Bhojani v. Ruff[[1997] A.J. 240 (C.A.)] is to the same effect Hunt, J.A., speaking for the court, found that it was proper for a taxation officer to decline jurisdiction where there was an apparent dispute between the parties as to the evidence. In that case, the parties were disputing the terms of the retainer agreement between the appellants and the respondent, including the proper amount payable by the appellants for legal services provided by the respondent. The court referred the matter back to the Court of Queen's Bench for resolution.
